:::{#def-dot-product}
#### Dot product
For any two real-valued vectors $\vx = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$ and $\vy = (y_1, \ldots, y_p)$
of the same length $p$,
the **dot product** of $\vx$ and $\vy$ is:

$$\vx \cdot \vy \eqdef \sumip x_i y_i$$

:::

::: notes

::: callout-note
The dot product $\vx \cdot \vy$ is a *linear combination*
of the entries of $\vy$, with coefficients $x_1, \ldots, x_p$.
It is also the standard *inner product* on $\reals^p$;
"inner product" is the general notion,
of which the dot product is one example.

See also the definitions in 

- @dobson4e, Section 1.3 (equation 1.1, page 7)

- @mosaiccalc, chapter on vectors
<!-- The chapter link (Textbook/Linear-combinations/28-Vectors.html) returned
404 in CI on 2026-09-25, and www.mosaic-web.org is unreachable from agent

- [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_combination)

"Linear combination" can also refer to weighted sums of vectors,
or in other words matrix-vector multiplication.

The dot-product has a different generalization for two matrices;
see [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_product#Dyadics_and_matrices) for more.

:::

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-dot-product}
#### A dot product

For $\vx = (1, 2, 3)$ and $\vy = (4, 5, 6)$:

$$
\ba
\vx \cdot \vy
&= 1 \cd 4 + 2 \cd 5 + 3 \cd 6
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= 4 + 10 + 18
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 32
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-lincom-symmetric}
#### Dot product is symmetric

The dot product is symmetric:

$$\vx \cdot \vy = \vy \cdot \vx$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

$$
\ba
\vx \cdot \vy
&= \sumip x_i y_i
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\\
&= \sumip y_i x_i
&& \text{(products of numbers are symmetric)}
\\
&= \vy \cdot \vx
&& \text{(definition of the dot product)}
\ea
$$

:::
